# Diagnosing Clutch Release Noise on a Subaru Outback

A rhythmic squeak or chirping noise from the clutch release mechanism, which vanishes immediately upon applying pressure to the pedal, points directly to a specific mechanical interaction within the flywheel assembly. On your 2007 Subaru Outback with the 5-speed manual transmission, this behavior is diagnostic of friction surfaces rubbing against each other when the hydraulic or cable actuation is at rest, but separating once tension is applied.

The throwout bearing (also known as the release bearing) is the primary suspect. This component spins on its own shaft but also pushes against the pressure plate's fingers to disengage the clutch. When the pedal is fully released, the bearing sits in a neutral position where it may be lightly contacting the inner race of the pressure plate assembly or spinning freely against a worn bushing. If the bearing's needle rollers are dry or if the lubrication has degraded, this light contact creates that cricket-like squeak at idle. The moment you apply even slight pressure on the pedal, the clutch release fork pushes the bearing forward into its disengaged position, physically separating the noise-generating surfaces and silencing the sound.

A common misconception is that the entire clutch release mechanism needs cleaning or greasing. While corrosion can occur in older vehicles, modern Subaru throwout bearings are designed as sealed units. Attempting to open a standard sealed bearing to clean or re-lubricate it is generally inadvisable. The internal seals are critical; once compromised, contaminants will enter, and the bearing will fail prematurely. If the noise persists after cleaning the external linkage (the fork and pivot points), replacing the sealed throwout bearing is often the correct path rather than trying to service the internals of a non-serviceable unit.

Another possibility involves the dual mass flywheel (DMF). The DMF assembly on the 2007 Outback is complex, utilizing springs to dampen engine vibration before transferring torque to the transmission input shaft. Inside the flywheel housing, there are sliding surfaces and bushes that can wear out or develop dry spots. If these internal components are rubbing against each other when the clutch is engaged (pedal up), they will produce noise. Applying pressure on the pedal changes the load profile on the flywheel's internal dampers, potentially shifting the contact points enough to stop the squeak, even if the root cause is a worn damper spring or bushing inside the hub.

To distinguish between these two, listen closely when you shift into first gear while the clutch is disengaged (pedal up). If the noise stops completely without touching the pedal, but only when you move the shifter into gear (which pushes the transmission input shaft slightly), the issue is likely internal to the DMF. However, if the noise persists in neutral or any gear as long as the clutch is fully released, the throwout bearing remains the highest probability.

Before committing to a full replacement, inspect the pivot points of the release fork shown in your image. These bolts and bushings can corrode or become dry over time. A simple application of high-temperature grease on the external pivot bushings (if accessible without removing the transmission) can sometimes eliminate the squeak if the issue is purely mechanical binding rather than internal bearing failure. However, remember that once the transmission is dropped to access the clutch assembly, replacing both the throwout bearing and inspecting the flywheel for scoring or oil leaks from the DMF seals is usually the most cost-effective long-term fix. Ignoring a failing DMF can lead to catastrophic failure during high-load driving, whereas a throwout bearing typically fails with a distinct whining noise that grows in pitch as RPM increases.
